name: The P versus NP Problem
statement: If a solution can be checked quickly, can it also be found quickly? Nobody knows.
meaning: The problem asks whether every problem whose solution can be verified quickly can also be solved quickly. P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time; NP is the class whose candidate solutions can be verified in polynomial time. The question — does P equal NP? — is one of the deepest open problems in mathematics and computer science, and remains unsolved.
mechanism: Polynomial time is the standard proxy for tractable — running time bounded by a polynomial in the input size. Within NP sit the NP-complete problems, the hardest members: every problem in NP reduces to any one of them in polynomial time, so if a single NP-complete problem had a fast algorithm, all of NP would collapse into P. The Cook-Levin theorem established the first such problem, Boolean satisfiability, proving that any NP problem can be transformed into a satisfiability question — which makes finding a fast algorithm for it equivalent to settling P versus NP.

examples.text: Checking a completed jigsaw or a filled-in Sudoku is easy, but finding the solution from scratch can be enormously hard — the everyday shape of the gap between verifying and solving.

Boolean satisfiability, the travelling salesman decision problem, and generalised Sudoku are NP-complete: a proposed solution is quick to check, yet no known algorithm finds one quickly, and all share the same fate.
Modern public-key encryption relies on problems being hard to solve but easy to verify; were P shown to equal NP with a practical algorithm, much of that security could unravel.

variants.name: NP-complete and NP-hard
variants.text: NP-complete problems lie in NP and are the hardest within it; NP-hard problems are at least as hard but need not lie in NP, or even be decision problems.

variants.name: The Cook-Levin theorem
variants.text: The foundational result establishing Boolean satisfiability as the first NP-complete problem, the anchor from which thousands of other problems were shown NP-complete.

whyItMatters: It is the central open question of computational complexity and one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize Problems, carrying a million-dollar prize. Its answer would reshape cryptography, optimisation, and our understanding of the limits of efficient computation — telling us whether creativity in problem-solving is fundamentally harder than recognising a good answer.

working.text: when facing a hard problem, distinguish how easily a candidate answer can be verified from how hard it is to find one.
if a problem is NP-complete, expect no known efficient algorithm and reach for approximation or heuristics instead.
treat P versus NP as unresolved — most believe P is not NP, but neither direction has been proved.

limits: This is an open, unsolved problem: no proof exists in either direction. The prevailing belief among theorists is that P is not NP — successive expert surveys put agreement above eighty percent — but belief is not proof, and flawed claimed proofs of both possibilities appear regularly, none accepted. The framework around it — the definitions of P, NP, NP-completeness, and the Cook-Levin theorem — is settled mathematics; it is the headline question itself that remains unresolved.
misreadings: It is not a solved or nearly-solved question — it is genuinely open, and 'P is not NP' is a widely held conjecture, not an established fact. And a proof that P equals NP would not automatically break all encryption overnight; the practical impact would depend on whether the algorithm it produced were efficient in practice.
origin: Formalised by Stephen Cook in 'The Complexity of Theorem-Proving Procedures' (1971), which proved satisfiability NP-complete; Leonid Levin reached the result independently, published in 1973, and it was named a Clay Millennium Prize Problem in 2000.
